source.title: A Simple Yet Effective Method for Non-Refusing Context Relevant Fine-grained Safety Steering in LLMs
source.authors: Shaona Ghosh; Amrita Bhattacharjee; Yftah Ziser; Christopher Parisien

record.tranche_reason: Tests transfer of harm-specific mean-difference steering vectors across model variants by applying Llama-2-7B-Chat-derived vectors to Llama-2-7B generations and reporting safety outcomes.
record.gate_note: The study measures unsafe-response rates and response quality for its own category-specific steering method, not refusal rates. It does not test ablating the original single refusal direction, adding it to harmless prompts, weight-editing it, or jailbreak suppression. Table 4 reports safety percentages for the method and baselines; the text also gives qualitative transfer examples and notes failures.
record.test_reason: The study builds a harmful-minus-harmless mean-difference steering method (SafeSteer) and reports only its own performance against naive generation and baselines (SEA, CAA). Its measure is the GPT-4-judged unsafe-response rate plus reward-model quality, and it deliberately avoids inducing refusals. It never ablates a direction, never measures refusal rates, and never tests whether refusal is mediated by one direction. The Chat-to-base vector transfer is a design choice to improve the method's own utility, not a test of whether the refusal direction carries across variants.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that category-specific, inference-time activation steering reduces unsafe outputs while staying on topic and avoiding blanket refusals. They report that transferring Llama-2-7B-Chat vectors improves helpfulness over baselines. They acknowledge the method is not reliable enough as a standalone safeguard, has failure cases, and covers only Llama models and a few categories.
record.recipe_differences: Uses harmful-versus-harmless mean-difference vectors, but constructs category-specific vectors and adds them to attention activations at selected layers; it does not ablate the original refusal direction or measure refusal rates.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by harm category, model, layer, multiplier, and vector-construction strategy. The paper reports that some transferred generations still fail to steer safely.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding category-specific harmful-vs-harmless mean-difference vectors to attention activations lowers GPT-4-judged unsafe-response rates. Examples: Llama3-8B 80.1%→0.67% and Llama2-7B 80.33%→58% on BeaverTails Child Abuse (Table 2/7). Helpfulness and coherence often drop.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harm-category-specific mean-difference activation vectors can steer models toward safe, non-refusing outputs, with effect size depending on model and category.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (2025)
record.problems: The evaluation covers a limited number of Llama-family models and harm categories, and the authors say the method is not reliable enough as a standalone safeguard. Transfer results are not accompanied by uncertainty estimates in Table 4; qualitative examples are selective. The study evaluates unsafe-response rates and reward-model quality rather than refusal rates.

untested.parts: No ablation of a refusal direction, no induced refusal on harmless prompts, no refusal-rate measure.
No jailbreak analysis or adversarial training.
Category-specific vectors are used, but there is no test of the geometry of refusal.
Harm judgment and refusal are not measured separately.
Chat-to-base vector transfer is used to improve steering quality, but no transfer of a refusal direction is measured. There are no cross-language tests.

record.verdict_notes: Arditi et al. is cited only as related prior work. The steering target is 'safety', not refusal, and refusal is explicitly avoided. The record's V6 'supports' labels rest on a method-versus-baselines table with an ambiguous subject, so they are removed.

versions.untested_parts: No ablation of a single refusal direction; no test of whether adding that direction makes the model refuse harmless requests; unsafe-response rate is not a refusal-rate measure.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration.
No test of attacks suppressing the direction or training against its ablation.
Category-specific steering vectors are used, but the study does not test whether refusal is affine, cone-shaped, or carried by multiple directions.
No separate measurement of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
No transfer across languages or model families; the reported transfer is across Llama-2 variants.
Does not compare how different refusal-training procedures or training stages determine whether a removable direction exists.

relation.reason: Cites Arditi et al. 2024 and Arditi & Obeso 2023 and builds on the mean-difference construction, but measures safety/helpfulness, not refusal, so it does not test the claim.

tranche.reason: Uses harmful/harmless mean-difference steering vectors (category-specific, token-averaged attention activations) as a tool. Reports only its own method's unsafe-response rate and reward-model quality, with no refusal rate, ablation or test of any version.

source_check.notes: Table 4 has no unsteered/naive column and conflicts with Sec 4.3 on the multiplier sign (-0.5 vs 0.5). Its generation model (Llama-2-7B vs Llama-2-7B-Chat) is ambiguous. The Chat-to-base vector transfer is near V6 but has no refusal measure, so verdicts of none are right.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Reported Llama-2-7B transfer results across the Table 4 categories
reader_labels.reason: Chat-derived vectors yield reported unsafe-response rates of 7.3%, 2%, and 2.7% in the target generations (r1-r3); the text also describes safe deflections in transferred examples (r4).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
